The general pattern is useful, but neurons differ enormously in shape, size, and function. Some are sensory cells that respond to the environment; others carry commands to muscles or communicate locally. Ramón y Cajal’s work helped establish that the nervous system is composed of individual cells rather than one continuous network. Connections between those cells are central to explaining behavior."},{"question":"Can you explain: Why glia matter?","answer":"Neurons are not the brain’s only important cells. Glial cells help regulate the chemical surroundings, provide support and insulation, participate in immune defense, and influence the conditions under which neurons can signal. Astrocytes interact with blood vessels and neurons; oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells form myelin in different parts of the nervous system; microglia contribute to defense and maintenance. It is misleading to imagine a brain in which neurons do everything and glia merely fill space. Neural activity depends on its supporting environment."},{"question":"Can you explain: The blood–brain barrier: protection and a trade-off?","answer":"The brain needs a highly regulated environment. Tight junctions among cells lining many brain blood vessels limit entry of numerous chemicals, protecting neural signaling from fluctuations and potentially harmful agents in circulating blood. Yet a barrier that blocks unwanted substances can also prevent useful medicines from reaching the brain. Important nutrients require suitable transport routes. The relationship between barrier and nourishment explains why not every chemical circulating elsewhere in the body can simply reach neurons."},{"question":"Can you explain: The brain and the rest of the body?","answer":"Neurons require energy and building materials, including oxygen and glucose under ordinary conditions. His observations changed how researchers could explain the direction of neural information flow.","paragraphIndex":20003,"bullets":[{"label":"Evidence","explanation":"Using microscopic staining and detailed drawings, Cajal examined the shapes and boundaries of neural cells; the patterns supported separation between cells.","paragraphIndex":20004},{"label":"Importance","explanation":"If neurons are separate units, communication between them needs an explanation. Understanding this machinery prevents treating an action potential as if it appeared without metabolic support.","paragraphIndex":20006,"bullets":[{"label":"Membrane and nucleus","explanation":"The plasma membrane controls exchange with the environment; the nucleus contains genetic information that guides protein production.","paragraphIndex":20007},{"label":"Energy and synthesis","explanation":"Mitochondria supply usable cellular energy; ribosomes assemble proteins, including components needed for receptors, channels and neural maintenance.","paragraphIndex":20008},{"label":"Membrane and nucleus","explanation":"The membrane is selectively permeable; channels and transport proteins regulate the movement of charged particles. The nucleus contains chromosomes bearing genetic information.","paragraphIndex":52204},{"label":"Protein and energy systems","explanation":"Ribosomes and endoplasmic reticulum help build and move proteins; mitochondria supply energy for cellular work. Neuronal signaling requires continuing metabolic support.","paragraphIndex":52205}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"A neuron's basic machinery resembles that of other animal cells. Their physical arrangement helps explain why changing a connection can change behavior.","paragraphIndex":20009,"bullets":[{"label":"Dendrites and soma","explanation":"Dendrites provide large surfaces for incoming synapses; the soma houses organelles and combines influences arriving from different sources.","paragraphIndex":20010},{"label":"Axon and terminals","explanation":"The axon conducts an electrical impulse, and its terminals communicate with target cells, usually through chemical release at synapses. Dendritic spines increase the surface available for inputs.","paragraphIndex":20011},{"label":"Receiving and integrating","explanation":"Dendrites and the soma receive many incoming influences; the cell combines these before producing an output.","paragraphIndex":52206},{"label":"Sending signals","explanation":"The axon carries information toward terminals that communicate with target cells. Myelin, when present, changes the speed and pattern of conduction. Not every neuron has a conventional long axon.","paragraphIndex":52207}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Neurons are specialized by the arrangement of their cell body, dendrites, axon, and presynaptic endings. A sensory neuron may have receptors at one end, while a motor neuron connects spinal circuitry with muscle.","paragraphIndex":20012,"bullets":[{"label":"Form follows function","explanation":"Cell shape influences where the neuron can receive messages and where its output travels. Shape alone does not tell us the entire function, but it constrains connections.","paragraphIndex":20013},{"label":"Different scales","explanation":"Long projecting cells relay information over distance; compact local cells can integrate signals within a small region without a long axon.","paragraphIndex":20014},{"label":"Form follows connectivity","explanation":"Shape affects where a neuron receives input and where it can send output.","paragraphIndex":52208},{"label":"Interpretation","explanation":"Do not assume every cell has the same number of dendrites, the same axon length, or the same response pattern. Some form the myelin that insulates axons.","paragraphIndex":20016},{"label":"Broader principle","explanation":"An explanation of behavior that counts neurons but ignores their supportive cellular environment is incomplete.","paragraphIndex":20017},{"label":"Support and regulation","explanation":"Glial functions include metabolic assistance, controlling the extracellular environment, immune-related responses, and producing myelin in relevant parts of the nervous system.","paragraphIndex":52210},{"label":"Importance to behavior","explanation":"Neurons depend on these surrounding conditions to communicate reliably. This protects sensitive neural signaling but also complicates delivery of drugs to the brain.","paragraphIndex":20018,"bullets":[{"label":"Selective access","explanation":"Not every substance that reaches blood can reach brain tissue. Barrier properties differ from the exchange that occurs through most ordinary capillaries.","paragraphIndex":20019},{"label":"Trade-off","explanation":"Keeping toxins and unstable chemicals out supports neural function, but some needed nutrients require regulated transport and many potential medications cross poorly.","paragraphIndex":20020},{"label":"Selective access","explanation":"Many molecules in ordinary blood cannot enter the brain freely.","paragraphIndex":52212},{"label":"Not a complete wall","explanation":"The system permits necessary materials through appropriate transport mechanisms, and its properties differ in some brain regions. The crucial principle is selective exchange, not absolute isolation.","paragraphIndex":52213}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"The blood–brain barrier regulates which substances can pass from circulating blood into brain tissue. The barrier is one layer of protection against sudden chemical variations elsewhere in the body.","paragraphIndex":20021,"bullets":[{"label":"Chemical stability","explanation":"Changing extracellular ions would change how readily neurons fire; limiting rapid fluctuations supports reliable communication.","paragraphIndex":20022},{"label":"Medical relevance","explanation":"A medication effective in a test tube may fail in the brain if it cannot reach neural tissue in sufficient amounts.","paragraphIndex":20023},{"label":"Protection","explanation":"Limiting entry of pathogens and some circulating chemicals reduces risks to sensitive neural tissue.","paragraphIndex":52214},{"label":"Trade-off","explanation":"The barrier also prevents some therapeutically useful substances from entering the brain easily. Protection and access must be balanced biologically.","paragraphIndex":52215}],"status":"original_classroom_note_sample","basis":"provided_book_pdf_and_markdown","followUpExplanation":"Neurons are especially difficult to replace after injury, so controlling exposure to potentially harmful material is important. Entry is selective rather than a total isolation from the body.","paragraphIndex":20024,"bullets":[{"label":"Tight junctions","explanation":"Adjacent endothelial cells seal many routes that permit substances to pass easily in other tissues.","paragraphIndex":20025},{"label":"Transport mechanisms","explanation":"Specific carriers allow essential molecules to enter; fat-soluble molecules can cross more easily than many water-soluble compounds, and some brain regions have special permeability.","paragraphIndex":20026},{"label":"Tight junctions","explanation":"Close contacts between endothelial cells restrict substances from slipping through gaps between them.","paragraphIndex":52216},{"label":"Transport routes","explanation":"Certain nutrients and other necessary molecules enter through regulated carrier systems rather than free diffusion. Neurons need a continuous, suitable fuel supply.","paragraphIndex":20027,"bullets":[{"label":"Fuel delivery","explanation":"Glucose and oxygen support energy production; transport systems help provide nutrients without allowing uncontrolled blood chemistry into the brain.","paragraphIndex":20028},{"label":"Vulnerability","explanation":"Interrupted blood flow or oxygen delivery can rapidly disrupt neural activity because energy reserves are limited.","paragraphIndex":20029},{"label":"Fuel use","explanation":"Glucose is the major normal fuel discussed in the text; ketones and lactate can also contribute under some conditions.","paragraphIndex":52218},{"label":"Physiological implication","explanation":"Ion gradients and synaptic signaling require energy. This protects sensitive neural signaling but also complicates delivery of drugs to the brain.","Not every substance that reaches blood can reach brain tissue. Barrier properties differ from the exchange that occurs through most ordinary capillaries.","Keeping toxins and unstable chemicals out supports neural function, but some needed nutrients require regulated transport and many potential medications cross poorly.","Neurons work only when concentrations of ions and neurotransmitters remain tightly controlled. The barrier is one layer of protection against sudden chemical variations elsewhere in the body.","Changing extracellular ions would change how readily neurons fire; limiting rapid fluctuations supports reliable communication.","A medication effective in a test tube may fail in the brain if it cannot reach neural tissue in sufficient amounts.","The barrier depends on the structure of the brain's capillaries and surrounding cells. Entry is selective rather than a total isolation from the body.","Adjacent endothelial cells seal many routes that permit substances to pass easily in other tissues.","Specific carriers allow essential molecules to enter; fat-soluble molecules can cross more easily than many water-soluble compounds, and some brain regions have special permeability.","The nervous system uses a disproportionate share of the body's energy because ion gradients and signaling require constant maintenance. Neurons need a continuous, suitable fuel supply.","Glucose and oxygen support energy production; transport systems help provide nutrients without allowing uncontrolled blood chemistry into the brain.","Interrupted blood flow or oxygen delivery can rapidly disrupt neural activity because energy reserves are limited.","Kalat introduces the gut microbiome to show that cells outside the brain can influence neural processes and behavior. The connection does not mean every behavioral problem originates in the gut.","Gut organisms affect digestion, metabolism and immune activity; these processes can send signals that influence the nervous system.","Associations between gut bacteria and behavior must be distinguished from evidence that changing a microbial population causes a particular psychological effect.","The cellular story links structures with mechanisms: neurons communicate, glia maintain conditions, and selective barriers keep the chemical environment workable.","Cell membranes, mitochondria, axons, glia and nutrient delivery are interdependent; disruption of one component can impair the whole network.","The action potential depends on membrane proteins and ion gradients, so electrical signaling is an extension of cell biology rather than a separate mystery."],"classroomResearch":{"title":"Essential historical evidence: Ramón y Cajal","body":"Microscopic observations of stained nervous tissue supported the view that individual neurons are distinct cells, challenging earlier network-as-continuous-mesh proposals. The lesson is methodological: microscopy turned a theoretical dispute about the nervous system into a question that could be evaluated against visible structure.","printedPages":[15,16],"pdfPages":[33,34],"kind":"essential_research_only"},"classroomCoverage":{"status":"expanded_three_chapter_sample","level":"comprehensive_masters_expanded","topicHeadings":12,"bullets":48,"newWords":1629,"allTopicsWithExplanations":true,"sourceScope":"provided_textbook_pdf_and_markdown","extendedWords":885},"classroomFigures":[{"id":"figure-1-10-11","headingId":"bp14-m1-2-h04","number":"1.10–1.11","title":"Motor and sensory neuron anatomy","printedPage":17,"pdfPage":35,"alt":"Two textbook diagrams labeling structures of a motor neuron and a sensory neuron; Action Potential","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":25,"printedEnd":38,"pdfStart":43,"pdfEnd":56,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"A resting neuron maintains an electrical difference across its membrane. Changes in sodium and potassium movement produce an action potential, which follows an all-or-none pattern rather than becoming larger with a stronger stimulus."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Track the sequence from resting potential to propagation and recovery. The refractory period, myelin, saltatory conduction, and local neurons help explain how neural signaling can be both reliable and suited to different distances."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m1-3-study-1","text":"From resting potential to a signal"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Even when it is not firing, a neuron maintains an electrical potential across its membrane. Selective permeability, ion concentration differences, and membrane pumps help create this resting potential. Sodium ions are usually more concentrated outside the cell and potassium ions more concentrated inside. When stimulation moves membrane voltage toward threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium enters rapidly, producing the rising phase of an action potential. Potassium conductance then helps restore the electrical state. This is a brief, regenerated event, not a packet of electricity simply leaking along a wire."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m1-3-study-2","text":"All-or-none does not mean every stimulus is equal"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Once an action potential begins, its size is fairly stereotyped for a particular axon: a stronger stimulus does not produce a proportionally taller action potential. Instead, stimulus intensity can influence how frequently a neuron fires or how many neurons become active. An action potential travels because a changed membrane region activates adjacent membrane. The process regenerates the signal along the axon, avoiding the loss that would occur if signals simply spread passively over a long distance."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m1-3-study-3","text":"Refractory period and direction"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Immediately after an action potential, sodium channels temporarily become unavailable and membrane conditions need time to recover. During the absolute refractory period, a second action potential cannot begin at that region; during the relative refractory period, it is harder to trigger one. These periods limit firing rate and help explain why a normal action potential propagates forward from the active region rather than repeatedly cycling backward. Separate the timing of the membrane event from the overall message carried by a train of such events."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m1-3-study-4","text":"Why myelin makes a difference"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Myelin insulates portions of many axons. The membrane is exposed at nodes of Ranvier, so action potentials are renewed at spaced intervals, a pattern called saltatory conduction. This makes long-distance signaling faster and more energy-efficient than repeatedly regenerating the signal over every small membrane segment. Not every neuron uses myelinated long axons: local neurons can process information over short distances with graded changes in membrane voltage. Distinguish such local potentials from the all-or-none signals of axons."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h01","text":"The Resting Potential of the Neuron"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"First, we need to consider the resting potential—the difference in electrical charge between the inside and the outside of a neuron.","sourcePrintedPage":25,"sourcePdfPage":43,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"All parts of a neuron are covered by a membrane about 8 nanometers (nm) thick.","sourcePrintedPage":25,"sourcePdfPage":43,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The inside of the membrane has a slight negative charge compared to the outside, mainly because of negatively charged proteins inside the cell.","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This difference in voltage is called the resting potential .","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The most common electrode is a fine glass tube filled with a salt solution.","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Connecting the electrodes to a voltmeter, we find that the neuron’s interior has a negative potential relative to its exterior.","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h02","text":"Forces Acting on Sodium and Potassium Ions"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If charged ions could flow freely across the membrane, enough positive ions would enter to depolarize the membrane.","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, the membrane is selectively permeable , letting some chemicals pass more freely than others.","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the membrane is at rest, the sodium and potassium channels are closed, permitting almost no flow of sodium and only a small flow of potassium.","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The sodium–potassium pump , a protein complex, repeatedly transports three sodium ions out of the cell while drawing two potassium ions in.","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because of this pump, sodium ions are more than 10 times more concentrated outside the membrane than inside, and potassium ions are more concentrated inside than outside.","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The sodium–potassium pump is effective only because the selective permeability of the membrane prevents the sodium ions that were pumped out from leaking back in again.","sourcePrintedPage":27,"sourcePdfPage":45,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, some of the potassium in the neuron slowly leaks out, carrying a positive charge.","sourcePrintedPage":27,"sourcePdfPage":45,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the neuron is at rest, two forces tend to push sodium into the cell.","sourcePrintedPage":27,"sourcePdfPage":45,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sodium is positively charged, and the inside of the cell is negatively charged, mainly because of negatively charged proteins.","sourcePrintedPage":27,"sourcePdfPage":45,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The other force is the concentration gradient , the difference in distribution of ions across the membrane.","sourcePrintedPage":27,"sourcePdfPage":45,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h03","text":"Why a Resting Potential?"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The body invests much energy to operate the sodium– potassium pump that maintains the resting potential.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The resting potential prepares the neuron to respond rapidly.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Excitation of the neuron opens sodium channels, letting sodium enter the cell rapidly.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the membrane did its work in advance by keeping so much sodium outside, the cell is prepared to respond vigorously to a stimulus.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Compare the resting potential of a neuron to a poised bow and arrow: An archer who pulls the bow in advance and then waits is ready to fire at the appropriate moment.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The resting potential remains stable until the neuron is stimulated.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h04","text":"The Action Potential"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If we now use a different electrode to increase the negative charge, we can produce hyperpolarization , which means increased polarization.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Now let’s apply a brief current to depolarize the neuron — that is, reduce its polarization toward zero.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"With a slightly stronger depolarizing current, the potential rises slightly higher but again returns to the resting level:","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the potential reaches the threshold , the membrane opens its sodium channels and permits sodium ions to flow into the cell, driving the membrane potential upward, far beyond what the stimulus itself provided:","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Any subthreshold stimulation produces a small response that quickly decays.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Any stimulation beyond the threshold, regardless of how far beyond, produces a big response like the one depicted, known as the action potential.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The peak of the action potential, shown as 1 30 mV in this illustration, varies from one axon to another, but it is consistent for a given axon.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h05","text":"The All-or-None Law"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Any depolarization that reaches or passes the threshold produces an action potential.","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For a given neuron, all action potentials are approximately equal in amplitude","sourcePrintedPage":28,"sourcePdfPage":46,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Slight variations occur spontaneously, but not because of the stimulus.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"More properly stated, the all-or-none law is that the amplitude and velocity of an action potential are independent of the intensity of the stimulus that initiated it, provided that the stimulus reaches the threshold.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"By analogy, imagine flushing a toilet: You need to press at least a certain strength (the threshold), but pressing harder does not make the toilet flush faster or more vigorously.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The all-or-none law constrains how an axon can send a message.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"To signal the difference between a weak stimulus and a strong stimulus, all that an axon can change is the frequency of its action potentials, or their timing.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, a taste axon shows one rhythm of responses for sweet tastes and a different rhythm for bitter tastes .","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h06","text":"The Molecular Basis of the Action Potential"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A protein that allows sodium to cross is a sodium channel (or gate), and one that lets potassium cross is a potassium channel.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"At first, opening the potassium channels makes little difference, but opening the sodium channels makes a big difference, because both the electrical gradient and the concentration gradient tend to drive sodium ions into the neuron.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Of all the sodium ions near the axon, less than 1 percent cross the membrane during an action potential, and sodium ions remain far more concentrated outside than inside.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because of the concentration gradient, sodium ions would continue to enter the cell, except that the sodium gates snap shut at the peak of the action potential.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the potassium channels remain open after the sodium channels close, enough potassium leaves to drive the membrane back to its original level and then slightly beyond it.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"At the end of this process, the membrane has returned to its resting potential, but the inside of the neuron has slightly more sodium ions and slightly fewer potassium ions than before.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, excessive stimulation occurs only under abnormal conditions, such as during a stroke or after the use of certain drugs.","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h07","text":"Propagation of the Action Potential"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Remember, it is important for axons to convey impulses without any loss of strength over distance.","sourcePrintedPage":30,"sourcePdfPage":48,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The term propagation of the action potential describes the transmission of an action potential down an axon, just as propagation of an animal species is the production of offspring.","sourcePrintedPage":30,"sourcePdfPage":48,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In a sense, the action potential gives birth to a new action potential at each point along the axon.","sourcePrintedPage":30,"sourcePdfPage":48,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An action potential starts in an axon and propagates without loss from start to finish.","sourcePrintedPage":30,"sourcePdfPage":48,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cell body and dendrites do not conduct action potentials, but they passively register the electrical event that started in the nearby axon.","sourcePrintedPage":30,"sourcePdfPage":48,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This back-propagation is important: When an action potential back-propagates into a dendrite, the dendrite becomes more susceptible to the structural changes responsible for learning.","sourcePrintedPage":30,"sourcePdfPage":48,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Everything follows logically from the facts that voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels open when the membrane is depolarized, and that sodium channels snap shut at the peak of the action potential.","sourcePrintedPage":30,"sourcePdfPage":48,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h08","text":"The Refractory Period"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the action potential is at its peak, the electrical potential across the membrane is above the threshold.","sourcePrintedPage":30,"sourcePdfPage":48,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"period? (If it did, the membrane would go into permanent depolarization.) The reason is that, at the peak of the action potential, the sodium channels shut tightly and remain tightly shut for approximately the next millisecond.","sourcePrintedPage":31,"sourcePdfPage":49,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This period is the absolute refractory period , the time when","sourcePrintedPage":31,"sourcePdfPage":49,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After that millisecond, the sodium channels relax a bit, but the rapid departure of potassium ions has driven the membrane potential farther into negative territory than usual.","sourcePrintedPage":31,"sourcePdfPage":49,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"2 to 4 ms, the membrane is in a relative refractory period , when a stronger-than-usual stimulus is necessary to initiate an action potential.","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Thus, the refractory period depends on two facts: The sodium channels are closed, and potassium is flowing out of the cell.","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The answer is that the areas it just passed are in their refractory period.","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h09","text":"The Myelin Sheath and Saltatory Conduction"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the thinnest axons, action potentials travel at a velocity of less than 1 meter/second (m/s).","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"At that speed, an impulse along an axon between a giraffe’s spinal cord and its foot would take about half a second.","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"To increase the speed still more, vertebrate axons evolved a special mechanism: sheaths of myelin , an insulating material composed of fats and proteins .","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The best solution would be to station people at moderate distances along the route and throw the message-bearing ball from person to person until it reaches its destination.","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The same principle applies to myelinated axons , those covered with a myelin sheath.","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Myelinated axons, present only in vertebrates, are covered with layers of fats and proteins.","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In myelinated axons, the action potential starts at the first node of Ranvier .","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The action potential cannot regenerate along the membrane between nodes because the axon has few if any sodium channels between nodes .","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An axon that has lost its myelin is not the same as an axon that never had myelin, because the axon lacks sodium channels where the myelin used to be .","sourcePrintedPage":32,"sourcePdfPage":50,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h10","text":"Local Neurons"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many tiny neurons, called local neurons , have no axon and communicate only with their immediate neighbors.","sourcePrintedPage":33,"sourcePdfPage":51,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because they have no axon, they do not produce action potentials, and they do not follow the all-or-none law.","sourcePrintedPage":33,"sourcePdfPage":51,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In such a cell, greater amounts of stimulation produce greater depolarization, called a graded potential , that spreads over the surface of the tiny neuron, declining in strength over distance.","sourcePrintedPage":33,"sourcePdfPage":51,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most local neurons have inhibitory effects on neighboring cells.","sourcePrintedPage":33,"sourcePdfPage":51,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m1-3-h11","text":"In Closing: Neurons and Messages"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"But these physiological mechanisms are the building blocks that we need to understand before delving into synapses, the connections between neurons.","sourcePrintedPage":33,"sourcePdfPage":51,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Local neurons are difficult to study because it is almost impossible to insert an electrode into a tiny cell without damaging it.","sourcePrintedPage":33,"sourcePdfPage":51,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most of our knowledge, therefore, comes from larger neurons, and that bias in our research methods may have led to a misconception.","sourcePrintedPage":33,"sourcePdfPage":51,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Meaningful thoughts and activities require activating some neurons and inhibiting others, and the inhibition is just as important as the excitation.","sourcePrintedPage":33,"sourcePdfPage":51,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the laboratory, researchers can apply an electrical stimulus at any point along the axon, making action potentials travel in both directions from the point of stimulation.","sourcePrintedPage":34,"sourcePdfPage":52,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"That is about one ten-thousandth the width of a human magnitude varies, but a typical level is 2 70 millivolts (mV).","headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h01","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44},{"type":"bullet","text":"Oxygen, carbon dioxide, urea, and water 1.21.","headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h02","sourcePrintedPage":26,"sourcePdfPage":44},{"type":"bullet","text":"Sodium is more concentrated outside than inside, so just by the laws of probability, it is more likely to enter the cell than to leave.","headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h02","sourcePrintedPage":27,"sourcePdfPage":45},{"type":"bullet","text":"Let’s begin by considering what happens when the resting else.","headingId":"bp14-m1-3-h05","sourcePrintedPage":29,"sourcePdfPage":47},{"type":"bullet","text":"A neuron’s membrane contains cylindrical proteins, like the ones in Figure 1.19, with different Selective permeability, ion concentration differences, and membrane pumps help create this resting potential. Sodium ions are usually more concentrated outside the cell and potassium ions more concentrated inside. This makes long-distance signaling faster and more energy-efficient than repeatedly regenerating the signal over every small membrane segment.
